relationship: Same-chapter introduction of Micah and arrival at his home
rationale: The opening identifies Micah in Ephraim's hill country; the Levite's later journey reaches that same named man's house in that region, establishing their meeting place.

relationship: Same-chapter confession of taking silver and its return
rationale: Micah admits taking the eleven hundred pieces of silver, and the next unit reports his return of that same amount before his mother announces her intended use.

relationship: Claimed consecration for images contrasted with the image prohibition
rationale: Micah's mother claims to consecrate silver to the Lord for a graven and cast image; Deuteronomy calls a craftsman's graven and molten image an abomination and pronounces a curse on its maker.

relationship: Same-chapter announced image-making and reported manufacture
rationale: The announced intention to make images is followed by the caster making them for Micah's house. The eleven hundred returned pieces and two hundred given to the caster remain distinct amounts.

relationship: Household ephods in related accounts with different assessments
rationale: Micah's sanctuary contains an ephod and teraphim and has his son as priest; the earlier Gideon account expressly calls its ephod a stumbling block to Gideon and his household. The two ephods are not identified as one object.

relationship: Same-chapter successive priestly appointments at Micah's house
rationale: Micah first fills the hand of one of his sons, who becomes priest; he later fills the Levite's hand and makes the young man priest. The repeated action is recorded without declaring either appointment authorized.

relationship: Own-eyes conduct contrasted with an earlier command
rationale: Judges describes each person doing what was good in his own eyes when Israel had no king; Deuteronomy commands against each man doing what pleases his own sight in its worship instructions.

relationship: Same-chapter narrated Levite origin repeated in his own answer
rationale: The narrator places the young Levite at Bethlehem in Judah, and he identifies himself to Micah as a Levite from that place. No replacement of the source's Judah-kindred wording is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter search for a place and Micah's lodging offer
rationale: The traveler seeks somewhere to sojourn and reaches Micah's house; Micah then offers residence, a father-and-priest role, silver, clothing and provisions.

relationship: Same-chapter self-description corresponds to the narrated introduction
rationale: The man's answer that he is a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah repeats the origin and identity already given by the narrator, without resolving those descriptions into a new genealogy.

relationship: Competing father-and-priest offers at household and tribal scale
rationale: Micah offers the Levite a father-and-priest role for himself with specified payment; Dan later offers the same roles to a tribe and explicitly contrasts that with serving one house. No new salary is reported.

relationship: Same-chapter residence offer followed by a son's-place comparison
rationale: The Levite begins to sojourn with Micah after the offer of residence and support, and the account likens him to one of Micah's sons without describing a formal adoption.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated hand-filling action with a different priest
rationale: The appointment of the Levite as Micah's priest repeats the earlier hand-filling description used for Micah's son, preserving the difference between the two appointees.

relationship: Micah's confidence contrasted with his later loss
rationale: Micah says the Levite's becoming his priest proves the Lord has done him good; later he complains that his image and priest have been taken and asks what he has left. His confidence remains a character's claim.

relationship: Different supplied accounts of Dan's inheritance
rationale: Joshua reports Dan's seventh lot, cities and later Amorite pressure; Judges says no inheritance had fallen to Dan while it sought a dwelling. Both actual statements are retained without resolving their chronology or replacing their wording.

relationship: Same-chapter five scouts sent from and returning to the same towns
rationale: Five Danite men leave Zorah and Eshtaol to explore the land, and five men later return to their brothers at those same towns. The mission's personnel and origin connect its departure and return.

relationship: Same-chapter recognition and questions answered by the hired priest
rationale: The scouts recognize the Levite's voice and ask how he came to be there; he answers that Micah hired him and he became Micah's priest.

relationship: The Levite's hiring report recalls the earlier appointment
rationale: His explanation that Micah hired him as priest corresponds to the earlier offer of support, his residence and Micah's appointment of him. The source's own role descriptions are retained.

relationship: Same-chapter request for inquiry and the priest's reply
rationale: The scouts ask for inquiry about whether their journey will succeed; the priest answers with peace and a statement that their way is before the Lord. The narrative does not separately introduce a divine speech here.

relationship: Same-chapter priestly reply to the stated journey question
rationale: The priest's words about going in peace and their way before the Lord answer the request to inquire about the journey. His reply is not treated as an independently verified authorization for every later act.

relationship: Same-chapter reconnaissance conditions recur in the attack account
rationale: The scouts see Laish's confident people and their distance from Sidon; the later attack finds a quiet, confident people and explains the lack of rescue by distance and lack of dealings. The differing contact descriptions remain intact.

relationship: Same-chapter returning scouts correspond to the five-man mission
rationale: The five men's return to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol completes the mission sent from those towns, without expanding the expedition into a different number of scouts.

relationship: Same-chapter scouts repeat their observations while urging an attack
rationale: The report repeats the people's confidence, Sidonian pattern, distance and lack of Syrian dealings observed at Laish, then adds the scouts' call to arise and take the land.

relationship: Same-chapter claimed prospect of taking land and the narrated attack
rationale: The scouts predict entry upon a confident people and claim God has delivered the land; the later account records the assault, burning and settlement. The scouts' divine-delivery claim is not converted into a separate divine command.

relationship: Same-chapter six hundred armed men at departure and at the gateway
rationale: The six hundred Danite men leave Zorah and Eshtaol equipped for war and later stand equipped at the gateway, connecting the expedition's numbered force with its deployment at Micah's house.

relationship: Shared camp designation with different location descriptions
rationale: Both use Dan's Camp as a place designation. One locates the camp behind Kiriath-jearim; the other places Samson's activity between Zorah and Eshtaol. No new map or independent site identification is supplied.

relationship: Different arrivals at Micah's Ephraim hill-country house
rationale: The Danite party reaches Micah's house in Ephraim's hill country, the same named destination reached earlier by the wandering Levite. The travelers and their purposes remain distinct.

relationship: The scouts' object list recalls Micah's manufactured sanctuary objects
rationale: The scouts name an ephod, teraphim, graven image and cast image; the earlier account describes the images being made and the ephod and teraphim at Micah's sanctuary.

relationship: Visit to the Levite at the house where he had been installed
rationale: The Danites enter the young Levite's house, identified as Micah's house; the earlier appointment account places the young priest staying in Micah's house.

relationship: Same-chapter armed gateway force identified with the expedition
rationale: The six hundred Danites at the gateway have the same stated number and war equipment as the men who set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, without adding another force to the total.

relationship: Same-chapter discovered sanctuary objects are subsequently taken
rationale: The five scouts first draw attention to the ephod, teraphim and two images and ask what should be done; they later enter and take those particular objects while the priest stands with the armed men.

relationship: Same-chapter priest's objection answered with a new appointment offer
rationale: When the priest asks what the men are doing as they take the objects, they tell him to be silent and invite him to serve a tribe rather than one household.

relationship: The father-and-priest role is offered on a larger scale
rationale: Dan repeats Micah's father-and-priest language but contrasts serving a whole tribe with serving one man's house. Micah's earlier specified payment is not assumed to have been repeated or increased.

relationship: Same-chapter pleased response and departure follow the tribal offer
rationale: After the invitation to become the tribe's father and priest, the priest is glad, takes the listed objects and joins the people, narrating his response without declaring the choice righteous.

relationship: Same-chapter departing procession and Micah's rearward pursuit
rationale: The departing party places household and valuable property ahead before Micah's group cries out from behind after it has gone far. The arrangement is retained without assigning the unstated possessive to a particular owner.

relationship: Same-chapter Micah's pursuit explained by the loss he alleges
rationale: Micah and his household cry out after the Danites; his following complaint specifies that they took his image and priest, giving his stated reason for pursuing them.

relationship: Same-chapter question about Micah's outcry and his explicit answer
rationale: The Danites ask what is wrong and why Micah cries out; he answers by naming the image and priest taken from him and asking what he has left.

relationship: Micah's loss reverses his earlier expressed confidence
rationale: Micah had claimed that having the Levite as priest showed the Lord's goodness to him; he now laments losing his made image and priest. The comparison concerns his two statements, not an endorsed promise from God.

relationship: Same-chapter threat against Micah followed by withdrawal before greater strength
rationale: The Danites threaten Micah and his household's lives; he then sees that they are stronger and returns home. No actual attack on or death of his household is added.

relationship: Same-chapter retreat after the Danites' threat
rationale: Micah withdraws on seeing the Danites' greater strength after they warn that violent men may fall on him and endanger his household. The account reports withdrawal rather than a battle between them.

relationship: Same-chapter attack on the quiet people earlier observed by the scouts
rationale: The later expedition attacks Laish's quiet, confident people, recalling the scouts' earlier description of their confidence and isolation. The earlier reconnaissance is not treated as an ethical justification for the attack.

relationship: Same-chapter isolation in reconnaissance and in the explanation of no rescue
rationale: The reconnaissance stresses distance from Sidon and no dealings with Syria; the attack account explains no rescuer by distance from the Sidonians and no dealings with people. These actual differences are preserved.

relationship: City naming invokes Dan's place among Israel's sons
rationale: Judges names the city after Dan, said to be born to Israel; Genesis lists Dan among Jacob's sons through Bilhah and frames the sons as twelve. No replacement city name or maternal genealogy is introduced.

relationship: Gershom and Moses in the supplied priestly genealogy
rationale: Judges gives Jonathan's ancestry as Gershom and Moses; Exodus names Gershom among Moses' two sons. The stated Moses form is preserved without substituting another ancestor or fixing an independent chronology.

relationship: Micah's household image becomes an object established by Dan
rationale: Dan establishes Micah's carved image, recalling its manufacture for Micah's house and that household's shrine. The transition from household possession to tribal establishment is explicit without equating its priests' identities.

relationship: Shiloh as the location of God's house and the tabernacle
rationale: Judges dates Micah's image establishment to the days God's house was at Shiloh; Joshua places the congregation and Tabernacle of Testimony at Shiloh. No external date for the image's duration is calculated.

relationship: Recurring Levite and Bethlehem-Ephraim settings without personal identification
rationale: Both episodes place a sojourning Levite in a Bethlehem and Ephraim sequence. One becomes Micah's hired priest; this man has a Bethlehem concubine. The records do not identify the two Levites as the same person.

relationship: Same-chapter angry separation followed by an attempt at reconciliation
rationale: The concubine becomes angry and stays with her father for four months; her husband then goes to speak to her heart, reconcile and bring her back. Adultery is not substituted for the stated anger.

relationship: Same-chapter reconciliation journey responds to the stated separation
rationale: The husband travels with a servant and two pack animals to bring back the concubine after her four-month stay at her father's Bethlehem house, retaining the account's stated purpose and cause.

relationship: Same-chapter initial hospitality followed by an additional pressured stay
rationale: The father-in-law first hosts the man for three days; later he presses him to remain again when he rises to leave. The additional night does not replace the initial three-day notice.

relationship: Same-chapter request to eat before departure and the shared meal
rationale: The father asks his son-in-law to strengthen himself with bread before leaving, and the two then sit, eat and drink together before another invitation to lodge.

relationship: Same-chapter invitation to lodge and a further night's stay
rationale: The father asks the man to lodge that night and be glad; when the man rises to leave, his father-in-law presses him and he stays again.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated invitations to postpone the journey
rationale: An earlier departure is delayed by the father-in-law's pressure; the later evening invitation again asks the party to stay and leave early tomorrow. The occasions are not collapsed into one night.

relationship: Same-chapter fifth-day delay becomes the evening reason to stay
rationale: On the fifth day the father asks the man to eat and remain until the day declines; the next appeal cites that same declining day as a reason to lodge again.

relationship: Same-chapter final overnight invitation and the man's refusal
rationale: The father-in-law proposes another night and an early departure tomorrow, but the man refuses to lodge and leaves toward Jebus with his party.

relationship: Jebus-Jerusalem and the recorded Jebusite residence
rationale: The traveler reaches Jebus, expressly identified as Jerusalem; Joshua describes Jebusites living in Jerusalem whom Judah could not destroy. The related residence notice is retained without supplying an unrecorded conquest chronology.

relationship: Same-chapter suggested Jebusite lodging rejected by the master
rationale: The servant proposes lodging in the Jebusite city because it is late; the master refuses a foreigner's city outside Israel and proposes Gibeah instead.

relationship: Same-chapter preference for an Israelite city contrasted with its later violence
rationale: The master avoids a foreigner's city in favor of Gibeah; that city's lawless men later surround his host's house and demand him. The juxtaposition contrasts his chosen destination with the violence encountered there.

relationship: Same-chapter proposed Gibeah-or-Ramah lodging and arrival at Gibeah
rationale: The master offers Gibeah or Ramah as places to lodge; the journey then reaches Benjamin's Gibeah as the sun sets, identifying which proposed destination is reached.

relationship: Same-chapter sunset arrival and unsuccessful initial search for lodging
rationale: The party passes to Gibeah at sunset and turns into that city to lodge, but its initial wait in the square brings no invitation into a house.

relationship: City-square lodging contrasted with a host's invitation
rationale: Judges initially records no one receiving the travelers from Gibeah's square; Genesis shows Lot urging visitors who propose the square to lodge in his house. The later Gibeah host is not erased by the initial contrast.

relationship: Same-chapter host and traveler share an Ephraim regional connection
rationale: The old man is from Ephraim's hill country and sojourns in Gibeah; the traveler says his home is in Ephraim's remote hill country. A shared region is stated without inventing a family relationship.

relationship: Same-chapter origin-and-destination question answered with the journey account
rationale: The old man asks where the traveler comes from and is going; the reply names Bethlehem in Judah, his Ephraim home and his lack of lodging.

relationship: Same-chapter travel account develops the initial household setting
rationale: The traveler describes returning from Bethlehem to his Ephraim house, corresponding to the opening Levite's Ephraim residence and Bethlehem concubine. The actual house destination is not replaced with a sanctuary destination.

relationship: Same-chapter available provisions and the host's subsequent hospitality
rationale: The traveler says they have fodder, bread and wine and lack nothing; the old man nevertheless brings him inside, feeds the pack animals and shares washing, eating and drinking. No exhaustion of the travelers' provisions is asserted.

relationship: Hosts urge visitors away from overnight lodging in the square
rationale: The old man insists the traveler not lodge in the square and offers care; Lot likewise urges visitors who propose the square into his house. Their particular hospitality appeals correspond without identifying the hosts personally.

relationship: Household reception with foot washing and food
rationale: Judges records entry into the host's house, fodder, washed feet and a meal; Genesis records Lot's invitation to wash feet and his preparation of a meal. Their different household details remain distinct.

relationship: Host houses surrounded and guests demanded by the city's men
rationale: Both groups surround a host's house and demand the guests be brought out. Genesis explicitly says lie with them; Judges says know him before the later assault is narrated. The men and guest numbers remain distinct.

relationship: Hosts go outside and appeal against wickedness
rationale: Both hosts go outside to the surrounding men, address them as brothers and ask them not to act wickedly. The parallel concerns the appeals, not approval of the subsequent offers of women.

relationship: Women's exposure proposed in place of male guests
rationale: Both hosts offer virgin daughters in place of male guests; Judges includes the man's concubine with the host's virgin daughter, while Genesis names Lot's two daughters. Recording the proposed exchanges does not endorse them.

relationship: Sexual force against a woman compared with a law protecting its victim
rationale: Judges narrates the concubine's forced exposure and rape; Deuteronomy distinguishes the forced woman's innocence from the assailant's guilt. The law's betrothed woman and field setting are not equated with this concubine and city.

relationship: Rejected host appeals followed by sharply different outcomes
rationale: Both hosts face refusal by the crowd. Genesis then describes the guests pulling Lot inside and striking attackers blind; Judges narrates the concubine being put outside and raped. No shared rescue outcome is asserted.

relationship: Same-chapter the woman's fall at the house and her morning discovery
rationale: The woman falls by the gateway entrance as morning comes; the following unit shows her master finding her fallen by the door with hands on the threshold.

relationship: Same-chapter discovery at the threshold followed by explicit death notice
rationale: The master finds the concubine fallen at the door and tells her to rise; she does not answer, expressly because she has died. Her death is not left unstated in this edition.

relationship: The later testimony repeats the concubine's death
rationale: The narrative expressly says the concubine had died when she did not answer; the Levite later tells the assembly she was violated, mocked and died. No death during the later cutting is inferred.

relationship: Pieces sent through Israel as a summons in distinct episodes
rationale: The Levite sends twelve portions of his concubine through Israel; Saul later cuts two oxen and sends pieces with a warning summoning Israel. The human victim and animals, speakers and stated messages remain distinct.

relationship: Appeal for national counsel followed by assembly and testimony
rationale: The dispatched message asks Israel to take counsel and speak; the following assembly gathers as one man, asks where the wickedness happened and hears the Levite's account.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated as-one-man assembly language
rationale: The congregation assembles as one man from the named extent at Mizpah; a later notice again describes Israel's men gathering from their cities as one man. The two notices emphasize the stated communal gathering.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated four-hundred-thousand Israelite muster
rationale: Both notices state four hundred thousand sword-bearing men of Israel; the later one expressly excludes Benjamin and calls them warriors. No extra army is added by counting the repeated notices twice.

relationship: Same-chapter inquiry about the wickedness answered by the Levite
rationale: The assembly asks where the wickedness occurred; the murdered woman's husband answers with Gibeah, the surrounding men, her death and his dispatch of her pieces.

relationship: The Levite's lodging account recalls arrival in Benjamin's Gibeah
rationale: The Levite tells the assembly he came with his concubine to Gibeah in Benjamin to lodge; the narrative had recorded the party's arrival and attempt to lodge in that city.

relationship: The Levite's account compared with the narrated assault and death
rationale: The testimony recalls a surrounding crowd, the concubine's violation and death. Its additional claim that the men wanted to kill him remains his stated account; it is not inserted into the earlier crowd's quoted demand.

relationship: The Levite's dispatch report recalls the narrated cutting and summons
rationale: He tells the assembly that he cut the concubine and sent her throughout Israel's inheritance; the earlier narrative specifies twelve portions and the accompanying request for Israel's counsel.

relationship: Repeated appeal for Israel's word and counsel
rationale: The Levite asks Israel to give its word and counsel, repeating the earlier dispatched appeal to deliberate and speak concerning the woman. The two appeals connect the summons with the assembly's deliberation.

relationship: Same-chapter collective commitment followed by its expedition plan
rationale: The people jointly refuse to return to their own homes; they then specify an expedition against Gibeah and proportional provisioning for the force, developing the stated commitment into a plan.

relationship: Same-chapter expedition decision developed by its provisioning provision
rationale: The decision to go against Gibeah by lot continues into a plan for selecting men at stated proportions to obtain provisions for those dealing with Gibeah. No particular lot outcome is invented.

relationship: Same-chapter supply selection serves the named Gibeah expedition
rationale: The ten-in-a-hundred and corresponding supply quotas serve the expedition against Gibeah named in the preceding part of the same speech. The quotas are not converted into an unstated total supply force.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed unity formula recalls the initial assembly
rationale: The later gathering as one man repeats the initial congregation's as-one-man description at Mizpah, linking the city's assembled men with the narrated national mobilization.

relationship: Same-chapter delegated question followed by the demand for the offenders
rationale: The tribes ask Benjamin about the wickedness among them and then demand Gibeah's impious men for execution; Benjamin's refusal is reported rather than an agreed surrender.

relationship: Removal-of-evil language in distinct judicial settings
rationale: Israel's demand to execute Gibeah's impious men aims to remove wickedness from Israel; Deuteronomy's execution instruction ends by removing the evil one. The offenses and stated procedures are not identified as the same case.

relationship: Same-chapter refusal to surrender the offenders followed by military resistance
rationale: After Benjamin refuses its brothers' demand for the impious men, Benjamin gathers from its cities at Gibeah to fight Israel. The account's transition is from rejected demand to tribal battle.

relationship: Same-chapter selected seven hundred described by their weapon skill
rationale: The muster names twenty-five thousand swordsmen apart from Gibeah's seven hundred chosen young men; the continuation describes the selected men's both-handed skill and accurate slinging without replacing it with a one-handed description.

relationship: Benjaminite fighting groups described with both-hand and sling skills
rationale: Judges describes Benjamin's chosen slingers as skilled with both hands; Chronicles describes Benjaminite men joining David with right-and-left bow use and stones. The different groups and weapon descriptions are not made identical.

relationship: Same-chapter later muster repeats the assembled force's stated total
rationale: The later muster again gives four hundred thousand sword-bearing Israelites and expressly excludes Benjamin, clarifying the side counted in the earlier assembly notice without adding a second force.

relationship: Repeated leadership inquiry and Judah answer with a different opponent
rationale: Both ask who shall lead Israel into battle and receive Judah as the Lord's answer; the opening inquiry concerns Canaanites, whereas this one concerns Benjamin. The opponents are not conflated.

relationship: Same-chapter camp at Gibeah followed by battle formation there
rationale: Israel camps against Gibeah and then draws up there for war against Benjamin, connecting the named camp with the ensuing deployment rather than a different battlefield.

relationship: Same-chapter opening battle deployment and Benjamin's first-day result
rationale: Israel's formation against Benjamin at Gibeah is followed by Benjamin coming from the city and killing twenty-two thousand Israelites that day, distinguishing Israel's intention from its adverse outcome.

relationship: Same-chapter first and second Israelite defeats with distinct casualty counts
rationale: Benjamin kills twenty-two thousand Israelites on the first occasion and eighteen thousand on the explicitly named second day. The repeated losses retain their different numbers and days.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed formation after the first recorded defeat
rationale: Israel strengthens itself and forms again in the first day's place after the report of twenty-two thousand killed, showing renewed deployment following loss without asserting that the first day was a victory.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed permission to fight followed by another defeat
rationale: The Lord tells Israel to go up against Benjamin after its weeping inquiry; the second-day account still records eighteen thousand Israelite deaths. Permission here is not rewritten as an explicit victory promise.

relationship: Same-chapter second-day approach and its stated result
rationale: Israel approaches Benjamin on the second day; Benjamin comes from Gibeah that same day and strikes eighteen thousand sword-bearing men, supplying the narrated outcome of that approach.

relationship: Same-chapter second-day defeat recalls the prior Israelite loss
rationale: The second-day loss of eighteen thousand repeats Benjamin's earlier success against Israel but differs from the first occasion's twenty-two thousand. No replacement or merger of the counts is supplied.

relationship: Repeated whole-burnt-offerings-of-deliverance wording
rationale: The people offer whole burnt offerings of deliverance after their defeats and later build an altar and offer whole burnt offerings of deliverance. The supplied combined wording is not silently split into different offering classes.

relationship: Same-chapter ark notice continued by the priest's presence and inquiry
rationale: The notice that the covenant ark was there continues with Phinehas standing before it and the renewed battle inquiry. The two connected units identify the narrated setting without moving it to a different sanctuary.

relationship: Phinehas's stated genealogy and priestly setting
rationale: Both name Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron; Numbers records the priesthood covenant, while Judges places him before the ark during inquiry. The shared genealogy is retained without calculating a chronology.

relationship: Ambush against a city in related battle plans
rationale: Israel places ambushes around Gibeah; the Ai plan likewise positions an ambush behind a city while a second group approaches and withdraws. The two cities, opposing peoples and deployments remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter third deployment recalls the stated second-day battle
rationale: Israel draws up on the third day as before, recalling its earlier second-day approach and Benjamin's successful attack. The third-day numbering is retained without treating the earlier losses as additional third-day casualties.

relationship: City defenders drawn out while pursuing Israel
rationale: Benjamin is drawn from Gibeah along the roads while pursuing and striking Israel; Ai's inhabitants had likewise pursued Israel away from their city. The named roads and casualty figure belong only to Judges here.

relationship: Feigned flight invites an opponent's mistaken as-before comparison
rationale: In both plans the opponents interpret Israel's movement through an earlier flight, while Israel intends to draw them away from the city for an ambush. Gibeah's and Ai's distinct battle accounts remain separate.

relationship: Same-chapter previously set ambush advances from its stated position
rationale: The ambush set around Gibeah later advances from west of Gibeah as Israel forms at Baal-tamar. The supplied direction and place name are retained without substituting another edition's position.

relationship: Same-chapter unrecognized disaster later expressly perceived by Benjamin
rationale: The earlier account says disaster had arrived without being known; the later account expressly names Benjamin seeing that disaster had reached them. The earlier unnamed pronoun is not independently assigned a new speaker.

relationship: Same-chapter promised delivery followed by the Lord's routing of Benjamin
rationale: The inquiry receives a promise that Benjamin will be delivered the next day; the subsequent report attributes Benjamin's rout to the Lord. The reported twenty-five thousand one hundred belongs to this outcome notice.

relationship: Same-chapter casualty summaries with different stated totals
rationale: One summary states twenty-five thousand one hundred Benjaminite dead and the later summary states twenty-five thousand. The two actual totals are preserved without asserting a rounding rule or an invented missing group.

relationship: Same-chapter retrospective explanation of the deliberate giving of ground
rationale: The narrative explains that Israel gave ground because it trusted its ambush, corresponding to its earlier stated plan to flee and draw Benjamin out. The explanation is not treated as a genuine initial rout.

relationship: Same-chapter the prepared ambush rushes into Gibeah
rationale: The ambush previously set around Gibeah now rushes toward the city and strikes it, connecting the preparation and execution without inventing a different city assault.

relationship: Same-chapter arranged smoke signal and its visible ascent
rationale: Israel and the ambush arrange a smoke signal from the city; a later unit records the signal and pillar of smoke rising as Benjamin looks back at the city's destruction.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated casualty notice and Benjamin's interpretation
rationale: The two passages each report about thirty Israelite casualties and Benjamin's interpretation through the earlier defeats. The repeated account is not counted as an additional thirty deaths or made into a new battle day.

relationship: Burning-city smoke changes the two sides' perception of battle
rationale: Benjamin looks back at Gibeah's rising smoke; Ai's inhabitants similarly look back at city smoke while Joshua and Israel see the capture and turn to attack. Only Judges expressly records a prior arranged smoke signal here.

relationship: Same-chapter disaster recognized after the earlier unknowing notice
rationale: The earlier notice says disaster had arrived without being recognized; the later one names Benjamin seeing it as Israel turns back. The relation follows the account's recognition contrast rather than adding a new casualty total.

relationship: Same-chapter wilderness flight and the subsequent named pursuit
rationale: Flight toward the wilderness with battle overtaking the fugitives is followed by flight toward Rimmon and the stated road pursuit as far as Gadaam. The account's actual place forms remain unchanged.

relationship: Same-chapter wilderness retreat overtaken near Gibeah's east
rationale: The preceding account says the battle overtook those turning toward the wilderness; the next notice records Benjamin cut down and trampled opposite Gibeah on the east. No modern route or substitute direction is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter pursuit subtotals and the later daily total
rationale: The eighteen thousand fallen are followed by five thousand and two thousand pursuit losses and a stated twenty-five-thousand total. This account's sum is retained alongside the separate twenty-five-thousand-one-hundred summary.

relationship: Same-chapter named pursuit losses followed by the twenty-five-thousand summary
rationale: The five-thousand and two-thousand pursuit losses lead into the daily total of twenty-five thousand; with the preceding eighteen thousand, they form this account's stated sum. Gadaam and Rimmon are not identified with other places.

relationship: Same-chapter daily totals retained in their different supplied forms
rationale: The later twenty-five-thousand summary differs from the earlier twenty-five thousand one hundred. Neither number is replaced or silently harmonized into a new exact casualty count.

relationship: Rimmon survivors become the recipients of the later peace message
rationale: Six hundred Benjaminite men remain at the rock of Rimmon for four months; the congregation later sends a peace message to Benjamin at that rock. No additional survivor total is inferred.

relationship: Destruction of Benjamin's settlements and the later lack of women
rationale: The narrative records attacks on Benjamin's cities, livestock and everything found; the elders later ask about wives because women have disappeared from Benjamin. The link does not assign an unstated individual fate to each person.

relationship: Same-chapter wife-giving oath explains the later marriage dilemma
rationale: The oath at Mizpah forbids giving daughters to Benjamin; the later question about wives explicitly repeats that oath as the constraint. The account's human oath is not presented as a fresh divine command.

relationship: Repeated corporate weeping before God in the war's aftermath
rationale: Both describe the people gathering and weeping before the Lord or God; the earlier notice locates them at Bethel, while the later one names Mizpah and Bethel. These supplied location descriptions remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter national question followed by the removed-tribe lament
rationale: The question why a tribe should be visited in Israel is followed by the statement that a tribe has been removed. The relation preserves the unusual visited wording rather than replacing it with another reading.

relationship: Altar offerings repeat the earlier deliverance-offerings description
rationale: Both notices use whole burnt offerings of deliverance, once after the defeats and once after the later weeping. The phrase is preserved without importing a separate peace-offering label.

relationship: Same-chapter assembly-absence oath and action against the missing settlement
rationale: The oath threatens death for absence from the Mizpah assembly; the following inquiry identifies Jabesh-gilead's absence, and the congregation sends a force there. The congregation's action is not attributed to an unstated command from God.

relationship: Removed-tribe lament alongside an explicit surviving remnant
rationale: The people lament that a tribe has been removed, whereas the preceding account records six hundred Benjaminite men surviving at Rimmon. The lament is not rewritten as a claim that no Benjaminite remained alive.

relationship: Same-chapter stated oath constrains the search for wives
rationale: The question how to obtain wives for survivors explicitly invokes the earlier oath against giving Israel's daughters to Benjamin, linking the dilemma to its recorded human commitment.

relationship: Same-chapter suspected assembly absence confirmed by inspection
rationale: The inquiry identifies no man from Jabesh-gilead at the assembly, and the inspection repeats that no man from its inhabitants was there. No unstated exemption or additional absent town is supplied.

relationship: Same-chapter confirmed absence relates to the stated oath penalty
rationale: The inspection finding no Jabesh-gilead man in the assembly supplies the specific absence relevant to the earlier oath threatening death to those who did not come. The comparison records the oath rather than endorsing the ensuing violence.

relationship: Same-chapter broad attack instruction followed by its specified scope
rationale: The congregation first orders an attack on Jabesh-gilead including women and people; the continuation specifies every male and every woman who has known a male's bed. The subsequent distinction is not silently erased.

relationship: Different campaigns distinguish women by the stated male-bed criterion
